{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"SCOPe 2.08 shows that NAD(P)-using proteins are not one evolutionary group. For example, the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann fold is c.2 (SUNID 51734), the FAD/NAD(P)-binding fold is c.3 (SUNID 51904), and the NAD-binding domain of HMG-CoA reductase is superfamily d.58.20 (SUNID 55035) within the ferredoxin-like fold d.58 and even a different structural class. Occurrence in distinct folds—especially across classes—therefore supports independent, convergent acquisition of dinucleotide binding, driven by the same ligand's chemical and geometric constraints. It does not establish descent from one ancestral NAD(P)-binding protein.

The hierarchy matters: members of one family generally support relatively close homology; a shared superfamily supports more remote common ancestry; a shared fold without a shared superfamily indicates architectural similarity but is not, by itself, evidence of homology. Different folds make a common origin still less defensible. Conversely, divergence can explain different NAD(P)-dependent activities within an established homologous superfamily, but the cofactor alone cannot identify that superfamily.

NAD(P) is widespread, and short glycine-rich phosphate-binding patterns, cofactor-contact residues, and catalytic geometries can evolve repeatedly. A locally similar binding pocket or a few matching active-site residues may thus be analogous rather than homologous. A homology claim needs independent, domain-wide evidence: statistically significant sequence/profile similarity with adequate coverage beyond the motif, compatible domain boundaries and secondary-structure topology, an extended 3D alignment, and preferably phylogenetic consistency. Biochemical ligand or active-site evidence supports a functional hypothesis, not ancestry by itself.

Accordingly, one must not transfer substrate specificity, catalytic mechanism, NAD-versus-NADP preference, domain architecture, or precise active-site annotation merely because two proteins bind the same cofactor or share a local motif. Template selection should be based on a demonstrably homologous family or superfamily and an appropriate domain-level alignment; a cofactor-bound representative from another superfamily or fold is only an analogy/template for general chemistry. A representative domain also documents its own lineage and cannot be treated as proof that every member of its fold has the same function or binding specificity.","evidence_used":["Pretrained model knowledge","mcp__scope__get_scop_service_info — /api/v1/releases/current","mcp__scope__search_scop — /api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=NAD&mode=token&limit=50","mcp__scope__get_scop_node — /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51734 and /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51734/parents","mcp__scope__get_scop_node — /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51904 and /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/51904/parents","mcp__scope__get_scop_node — /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/55035 and /api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/55035/parents"]}]}
